The relations between the Drúedain and other peoples of Men have been deeply marked by persecution. Their appearance and customs long fuelled prejudices that contributed to their exclusion. In the lands around the White Mountains, the memory of past violence remains particularly strong, especially the deeds of Men who gradually occupied the Drughu's former territories.

In the Third Age, the Rohirrim know of the Wild Men of Drúadan Forest, but relations remain burdened by profound mistrust. The Drughu remember those who were hunted and treated like wild game. To a Drughân raised on such memories, meeting a rider of Rohan may stir fears and resentments handed down through generations.

Yet his people's history also preserves remarkable friendships. The bond between Aghan and Barach shows the deep loyalty the Drúedain could feel towards Men of other peoples. This dual inheritance lends the character an especially rich way of approaching strangers: the caution learned in childhood may slowly give way to trust founded upon deeds.

The War of the Ring marked a decisive turning point. When Théoden led the Rohirrim towards Minas Tirith, Ghân-buri-Ghân, chief of the Drúedain of Drúadan Forest, revealed ancient paths by which the riders could pass around the enemy's forces. His people's aid helped the Rohirrim reach the Pelennor Fields. After Sauron's downfall, Elessar recognised the Drúedain's right to live freely in their forest and forbade others to enter it without their permission.

The hatred of Orcs has still older roots. From the First Age, the Drughu fought the servants of Morgoth who threatened their communities. Attacks, destruction and poisons used by these enemies left deep marks upon their history. A Drughân who has witnessed such violence may harbour fierce hatred, tempered by the knowledge that his people's survival matters more than reckless vengeance.

His own powers may also attract covetous attention. The secrets of guardian stones or enchanted tattoos might interest an ambitious chieftain eager to strengthen his warriors, or a servant of the Shadow bent on turning these arts to evil purposes. A promise of power sufficient to protect his clan for ever can become a formidable temptation, especially while his people remain in danger.

The Great Brothers' tradition, however, is founded upon protection and the passing on of knowledge. Employing such lore for domination would betray their calling. This conflict provides a way to explore the dangers of the Shadow without treating the Drughân's own magic as inherently corrupt.

The Drughân Through the Ages

The Drughân's place in the world depends profoundly on the period in which the campaign is set.

In the First Age, he may dwell in the Forest of Brethil among the Drúedain who maintain close relations with the people of Haleth. His knowledge helps guard isolated dwellings, tend victims of Orc attacks and defend threatened lands.

In the Second Age, he may belong to communities dwelling in the White Mountains or along the western coasts. He witnesses the arrival of new peoples and the changes brought about by the spread of Númenórean settlements. Traditions recalling Drúedain who lived in Númenor offer further possibilities for campaigns set in this age.

In the Third Age, the Drughân often lives in an isolated community marked by memories of persecution and the danger of Orc incursions. His mistrust of outsiders may be profound. His calling as a guardian then assumes particular importance.

In the Fourth Age, Elessar's decisions make a different future possible. A Drughân may help protect the territories now recognised as belonging to his people, renew ties with neighbouring communities or seek knowledge lost over the centuries.

Each age therefore gives the character a different identity. A First Age Drughân may have grown up remembering the old friendships between the Drughu and the Haladin. One living in the Third Age bears the consequences of generations of persecution. A Drughân of the Fourth Age belongs to a generation beginning to imagine a new existence, founded on recognition of his people and preservation of their traditions.

Leaving the Forest

A Drughân's calling remains deeply rooted in his community. Leaving home is therefore a momentous decision, usually prompted by a particular duty, an urgent need or an event that has changed the course of his life.

Some are sent to seek a rare remedy, find a missing clansman or request aid from a foreign people. Others travel after their master's death, hoping to complete an unfinished education or recover traditions whose keepers have become scarce. An ancient guardian stone, abandoned during a migration, may likewise justify a long journey through unfamiliar lands.

Circumstances are sometimes more painful. A Drughân whose clan has been destroyed by Orcs must learn to live after losing those he had sworn to protect. Another has left following a dispute with the elders, or because he refuses to see knowledge disappear that his community can no longer preserve.

Discovering other peoples is then a profoundly new experience. Reactions to his appearance, tattoos or customs may revive the prejudice that the Drughu have endured for so long. Yet his skills also allow him to form relationships built on respect. A healer will value his knowledge of plants, a Ranger will recognise his gifts for watching and tracking, and a scholar may discover in his stories a history largely unknown to the peoples of the West.

Within a company of adventurers, a Drughân brings a singular kind of experience. Accustomed to watching his surroundings closely, he notices clues his companions might disregard. His caution may slow a march or delay a decision, especially when he suspects enemies nearby. Experience has taught him that recognising danger before meeting it often saves lives.

His traditions also shape his behaviour. Ancient places, abandoned sculptures and certain hunting practices carry meanings his companions will gradually come to understand. Disagreements arising from such matters may lead to particularly rich relationships, especially when he travels beside descendants of peoples who once persecuted the Drughu.

Adventuring also offers the Drughân a life different from the one he knew among his people. His companions come to know the man behind the guardian's duties, with his memories, affections, weaknesses and perhaps a quiet sense of humour contrasting with his customary reserve. New friendships can grow without effacing old loyalties.

Playing a Drughân

A Drughân might be a young initiate newly admitted among the Great Brothers, an experienced healer in search of an unknown remedy, a guardian who has lost his clan, or the keeper of a tradition his master charged him to preserve.

His character will largely depend upon his history. A man raised among a community threatened by Orcs may be fierce and suspicious, while a disciple who has known peaceful dealings with other peoples may meet strangers with curiosity. Some show great gentleness towards children and the sick; others exercise their responsibilities with a severity shaped by hardship.

His relationship with his master, his tattoo and the traditions of the Great Brothers deserves particular attention. Did he receive his mark with pride, or does it represent a burden he finds difficult to bear? Is there an ancient stone he has been entrusted to guard? Has he lost someone he believed he could save? Which teachings does he wish to pass on, and what knowledge will he refuse to share with strangers?

The reason for leaving home is equally important. It may be a mission, a debt, a personal quest or a desire to discover what has become of his ancestors' lands. Returning to his people after years spent among strangers may prove as significant as the adventures themselves.

The Drughân is particularly well suited to campaigns about travel, wilderness, ancient peoples and the effects of the Shadow upon isolated communities. His magic extends an extraordinary understanding of nature, while loyalty to the Drughu gives him responsibilities far greater than his own life.

He offers the chance to portray a character devoted to the memory of a long-despised people, whose encounters and personal choices may help prepare a different future for his kin.

Game Master's Note — The Drughân in MERP-RMU

The Drughân has particularly rich foundations in Tolkien's writings. In The Lord of the Rings and Unfinished Tales, the Drúedain are associated with exceptional knowledge of the wilderness, healing and remedies, stillness and concealment, and sculptures to which some could impart extraordinary power.

The Drughôr-ghan brotherhood in its game form, the six professional Spell Lists and the detailed system of magical tattoos extend this inheritance for roleplaying purposes.

In MERP-RMU, the Drughân is traditionally restricted to Drughu culture. He is a semi-spell-user of Channeling, with Intuition and Memory as his Prime Stats.

His six Base Spell Lists are:

Spell List Domain
Animal Mastery Approaching, calming and influencing animals
Herb Mastery Finding, preparing and enhancing herbal remedies
Nature's Lore Understanding the environment and natural phenomena
Nature's Movement/Senses Enhancing movement, perception and certain physical abilities
Nature's Protection Resisting and protecting against certain natural hazards
Plant Mastery Influencing the growth and restoration of plants

A special feature of the profession allows a Drughân to replace two of these six Lists with two professional Ranger Lists, in accordance with the module's character creation rules.

Sacred tattoos are another defining feature of Drughu tradition. Their acquisition and effects follow the Talents and mechanics actually available in MERP-RMU. Tattoo Crafts represents the knowledge required to create and enchant them and remains distinct from the six Base Lists.

Guardian stones are also part of the Drúedain's inheritance, but their magical creation should not be treated as an ability automatically available to every Drughân. Aghan's feat remains exceptional; the Game Master may reserve such achievements for particularly accomplished masters or extraordinary circumstances.

Finally, the Drughân is not inherently associated with the Shadow. His powers belong to a tradition of knowledge and protection. Any use of corrupted practices falls under the relevant Shadow and Corruption rules of MERP-RMU.

The Game Master may adapt ceremonies, tattoos and the Great Brothers' teachings to their own interpretation of the Drughu while preserving the essential features established by Tolkien.
